description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities. Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the Grant Obligations and Conditions, the obligatory dates for submission of the annual/additional reports are mentioned. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

**Output 1: Knowledge and skills of ABEM in digital engagement techniques is improved to enable ABEM to develop a youth engagement strategy that is inclusive and in line with needs of youth.**
Activities and results that contributed to this output:
**Three trainings**
The trainings were delivered by RNW Media and Yaga Burundi and were attended by 38 participants of ABEM. The participants were in the age of 18-35 and 50% identified with female and 50% with male.
++Training ‘Build your digital community’ ++This training introduced participants to the best practices on digital interventions and online sexuality education by highlighting insightful case studies from RNW Media network and beyond. The training touched upon ways to key into an audience, the advantages, and disadvantages of various digital channels, as well as the roles that need to design and maintain a successful and sustainable digital community. The training was delivered from 22-26 November 2021. Facebook post regarding the training: [https://bit.ly/3vd8UQq](https://bit.ly/3vd8UQq)
++Training ‘Storytelling to inspire social change’ ++This training focused on topics like, the value of storytelling, how and why to craft emotional appeals, write persuasive case studies and engaging formats. The training was delivered from 31 January to 8 February 2022.
++Training ‘Media campaigning for social change and advocacy’ ++The training strengthened the participants’ capacity to engage the public, stimulated an iterative process of campaign design and helped the participants to increase their campaign’s relevance, reach & impact. It also provided guidance on campaigns that aim to influence key stakeholders and decision-makers for the purpose of advocacy. The training was delivered from 9-13 May 2022. Facebook post regarding the training: [https://bit.ly/3mbEoED](https://bit.ly/3mbEoED)
For each training a pre-survey was used to assess the specific needs of the participants and the results were used to tailor the training. The trainings were delivered in a hybrid format, with one trainer online and one trainer being on location in person. After the training a post-evaluation survey was done. Below the results are summarized for the three trainings.
**Field visits**
To understand their audience better and know with which problems and misconceptions they are dealing, the participants conducted fields visits. 36 of the 38 participants visited four youth-friendly health centres in 4 different provinces of Burundi namely Ngozi, Gitega, Makamba, Kirundo. The 36 members were subdivided into 4 groups, one group per province. The overall objective of these visits was to inquire about the situation of SRHR services and the accessibility of SRHR information for young people in these region. During the visits members had discussions with the providers of the centres and organized a plenary session with young people. The participants assessed the current offer of SRHR services to youth, how these services are offered and what challenges there are for your people to access SRHR information and services.
**Gender policy and youth engagement strategy**
To contribute and ensure that content and youth engagement is inclusive and effective, ABEM developed two important administrative documents: the “Youth engagement strategy” and “Gender policy”. The Gender policy applies to all of ABEM’s operations throughout Burundi. It applies to the programmes they develop and implement, their communication and the work environment (structure, culture, partnerships) they operate. The document presents ABEM’s commitment, approaches and activities to include gender equality in the full scope of their work and work environment. The progress of and adherence to the policy will be monitored by focal points who are appointed in each unit of the organisation. Each year the gender policy will be reviewed by the focal points and adjusted via the Gender Community of Practice. The Youth engagement strategy has been incorporated in the field visit report.
**Output 2: ABEM increases the number of youth it reaches with comprehensive, correct information on sexuality**
**Online content and campaign.**
Thanks to the knowledge and skills gained through the trainings and with support from RNW Media (implementing partner Yaga Burundi), the participants were able to create SRHR social media content and publications. More than 50 publications have been made mainly Facebook posts and TikTok videos. Link to some content: [https://bit.ly/3xPe1rZ](https://bit.ly/3xPe1rZ) and [https://bit.ly/3YcFQns](https://bit.ly/3YcFQns)
The content reached and informed no less than 207,412 people on SRHR topics including early and unplanned pregnancies, menstruation and menstrual hygiene, GBV (Gender Based Violence), STIs and HIV, contraception, parent-child dialogue, etc. 4,391 young people reacted to the content and took actions amplifying ABEM’s content through comments, shares or likes on the publications made, extending the reach to even more people in Burundi.
An online campaign ([https://bit.ly/3kydBSq](https://bit.ly/3kydBSq)) on “Relationships and how young people experience them” was carried out, jointly by ABEM and Yaga Burundi and reached 505,936 people among them 67,449 engaged by strengthening our messages either by likes, shares or comments.
**Health clubs**
Secondary students received information on SRHR topics during Health clubs. 1400 young people from 11 schools engaged in these health clubs. Before the project, ABEM was intervening in seven schools and four were added during this project. Questions and/or observations raised during discussions, hence what young people really want to know, informed and inspired online content creation to be published later online. On the other hand, online content, mainly videos, were used as teaching materials during the in-person sessions. Whereby offline and online activities were complementary.
**Recommendation paper**
On top of the above mentioned activities ABEM developed a recommendation paper with the aim to inform stakeholders on the current access and quality of SRHR information for young people in Burundi and provide recommendations how to improve. The paper is disseminated to all stakeholders in the sexual and reproductive health of young people in Burundi, including the Ministry of Public Health and the Fight against AIDS, the Ministry of National Education, various youth organizations, religious organizations, parents and the media.

**Project team set-up (July - August 2021)** In July 2021 we established the project team coordinating this project, including both members of ABEM as well as staff of RNW Media. We started with weekly meetings to get to know one another and to unpack the proposal and local context further. We met with a few challenges in this phase, leading to some delays:
- ++Language barrier. ++Not all members had the same level of French or English proficiency. We added francophone RNW Media staff members to the team team members this challenge was mitigated to some extend. To support ABEM with English proficiency we sought support from our in-country partner Yaga Burundi. - ++Lack of internet access++: ABEM met with some challenges with internet connection. We decided to extend some funding to purchase a router for use during training courses, as offline training still wasn't possible due to COVID regulations. To tackle the challenges with internet access in the organisation ABEM started to use the network of Yaga Burundi. - ++Understanding the local context:++ ABEM informed RNW Media in more detail about the local context and challenges that youth phase when it comes to SRHR and CSE. By adding a RNW Media team member with prior experience in projects on CSE/SRHR in Burundi the team was completed.
**Project implementation plan (September - October 2021) **In September 2021 we started to unpack the proposal and develop a more detailed project implementation plan and workplan and started preparatory activities:
- ++Define training course++ content objectives and content. This was done through intensive conversations between RNW Media and ABEM about the needs ABEM assessed within its organisation. The insights of Yaga Burundi about the local context and their view of needs of ABEM as organisation helped to focus and develop the training course outline. - ++Select participants:++ ABEM selected the participant based upon the selection criteria set in the proposal. These criteria were rediscussed with RNW Media's Course Coordinator to ensure proper alignment between training portfolio and paticipants profile. We decided to select 38 partipants rather than 32, due to other obligations that participants might phase. With participants being students and interns working in the medical sector, the workload might be too intensive for some. - ++Select trainers++: We discussed training content and timing with the selected trainers (as represented in the proposal). All trainers seem to be a good fit to training content and are available. Some gaps in their expertise will be filled by inviting matching local trainers (mostly from Yaga Burundi) - ++Align with local university++: To ensure alignment between programme planning and school exams, we connected with a professor at the University of Burundi. By including him in the project, will help us in aligning project planning as well as in project outreach and advocacy within the context of the university. - ++Revisions in budget and logframe ++Based on the new insights the project budget and logframe were redefined and shared with Nuffic. - ++Pre-course survey: ++ To better understand the needs and prior experience of the particpants we conducted a pre-course survey. Results were used to refine the training content in line with expectations and needs. - ++COVID related challenges:++ - _Quarantine for international trainers: _Due to COVID regulations the selected international trainers are not able to travel to Burundi. It would take too much of their time to be in quarantine. At the same time the participants seem to phase issues with internet access or connection. To tackle this challenge we decided to host each training in a blended on/offline format. We will invite the participants to be physically together in a training room during the trainings, enable internet access through providing a router from the training budget, yet enable the international trainer to join online. The local trainer will guide the participants throught the online elements and help them with offline assignments and communication - _Availability of participants offline: _Participant work (as interns) in the medical sector. This presents a couple of challenges in this project. The workload in this sector is high, whih might lead to limited availability. And at the same time they might have a higher chance to be infected, not being able to join the training. By selecting more participants we hope that in the end we meet targets and have 32 certified participants. By providing the training online (as well as offline) we allow participants in quarantine to remain in touch with training content. - _Redefine training planning in alignment with education obligations, like exams. _Covid let to delays and restrictions, leading to a re-adjusted training planning. We defined a training planning in alignment with the universities from which the participants are coming from. Based on the planning of exams we decided to host a first training in November 2021 and continue with training weeks in Februari and March 2022. The advocacy and campaiging activities will start in January and end in December 2022.
**Local coordination (September - October 2021) **As becomes apparent above, we met with some challenges in local coordination. With ABEM team being fully engaged in sstudy, internship, work and voluntairy work, they are limited available to take up local coordination. The would be able if the would be paid for the hours spend on this project. As that is not possible within Nuffic Orange Knowledge Programme funding criteria, we asked Yaga Burundi to support us in local implementation and coordination of the project. In close collaboration with ABEM Yaga Burundi developed a Workplan, including a detailed overview of activities, roles and responsibilities and a GANTT chart and budget. Based on this plan we contracted Yaga Burundi as local implementing partner. Their tasks will be to ensure local training venue and materials, coach ABEM in organisational development, support participants and take their learning curve beyond the trainings. The Workplan will be shared.
**First training: November 2022 **The first training took place 22-25 November 2022. Participant satifaction rate was 8,56 and attendance was 95%
